body_markdown:
People are always talking about their bucket lists. Things they want to do before they die. I have no bucket list, which might seem strange for an obsessive car collector, but there you have it. If I was forced to come up with something? I really don’t want to die by misadventure. Like tripping over a bucket, tragically placed, and kicking it.


I will admit, though, I’ve always had a hankering to go to the Bonneville Salt Flats, to see what it’s all about. And, as luck would have it, a couple weeks ago, JCB, the venerable British maker of construction equipment, invited me to join its people there for three days at the annual Bonneville Speed Week. I’m glad I went.


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Founded in a humble shed on the heels of the Second World War, JCB has grown to be a powerhouse in its field. Lately, it has developed a hydrogen-fueled, spark-ignition version of its stout, in-house four-cylinder diesel. It plans to offer the engine as an option across much of the company portfolio, from backhoes to generators. But the reason JCB called me was because it was eyeing a new land speed record for said hydrogen mill, with outright record holder Briton Andy Green set to take the controls of the long (32 feet), narrow (44 inch), and sleek, twin-engine streamliner called Hydromax. Appearance-wise, it’s as far away from one of JCB’s front-loaders and backhoes (the English call them diggers) as the Sun is from the Earth.


JCB


JCB


JCB


The simile is apropos, because the Sun, with all its searing heat and blinding glare, amplified by the white salt surface of the flats, is a big part of the Bonneville experience. So is the salt, underscored on the drive out from Salt Lake City when we pass a Morton salt plant and again when my knowledgeable driver relates the fascinating history of the local brine shrimp industry. You might know them as the “sea monkeys” once advertised in the back of comic books, along with X-Ray specs and whoopee cushions, but today they’re mostly breakfast, lunch and dinner for farmed shrimp and fish.


Jamie Kitman


Arriving at the Flats, we are greeted by preternaturally flat and, you guessed it, salt-encrusted land, as far as the eye can see. As the business of Bonneville Speedweek carries on off in the distance, all manner of RVs and trailers are randomly parked by the side of the salty trail we bounced along, headed for the mercifully air-conditioned JCB tent closer to the starting line.


JCB


JCB


Jamie Kitman


Inside we find a veritable army of skilled personnel from the U.K., who toggle between here, the starting line and an impromptu but well-equipped garage lashed up in an old airplane hangar at Wendover Airport, adjacent to a WWII airfield in Wendover, Utah. Later we’d meet Green, a former RAF wing commander who set the land speed mark twenty-nine years ago in the Thrust SSC. Powered by twin turbofan fighter jet engines, Green conducted that brute to a two-way average speed of 763.03 miles per hour in 1996, setting a record that stands to this day. For those keeping score at home, he remains the only person on the planet to break the sound barrier on land, ever.


JCB


Twenty years after that momentous achievement, Green went on to set the land speed record for diesel, shattering the old mark of 237 mph in JCB’s Dieselmax at a comparatively relaxed 350.09 mph, another record that still stands. The Hydromax borrows much from Dieselmax, with which it broadly shares its outward appearance, though it is longer and a useful 10 percent more slippery.


JCB


JCB


The hydrogen-fueled engine is a race-prepared, 4.8-liter version of the basic 4.4-liter engine available in much of JCB’s construction equipment line. In diesel form, it’s a torque monster with up to 406 lb-ft, yet it churns out only between 74 and 173 horsepower, quite a bit off the turbocharged and intercooled spark-ignition Hydromax’s 798.5-horsepower engines. Multiplied by two with one engine to drive the front wheels through a six-speed transmission and another identical one (with its own transmission) for the rears, we’re talking 1597 horsepower of all-wheel-drive thrust. In other words, important elements of Hydromax’s ability to break the Southern California Timing Association’s (SCTA) class record for Blown Gas Streamliners (AA/BGS, 500+ cubic inches).


Which it later did at 368.347 mph, making it the fastest zero-emissions car in the world, before setting an FIA world land speed record for hydrogen-powered cars seven days later at an even more impressive 406.320 mph.


JCB


In addition to the joy of setting new records, JCB hoped to showcase the practical aspects of hydrogen as a combustion fuel, rather than using it as part of a fuel cell car, particularly in the conscribed realm in which it competes. Construction vehicles typically don’t go far under their own steam and are refueled on site. A JCB hydrogen storage trailer capable of filling its vehicles in ten minutes compares not too unfavorably with diesel top-ups and represents a less time-consuming process than recharging batteries. And, of course, hydrogen vehicles’ only emission is steam, addressing a real concern in the many countries around the world as they begin demanding zero emissions from not just cars but off-road equipment. Should America become one of these countries, an existing JCB factory in Savannah, Georgia, and a new one currently being erected in San Antonio, Texas, would be well-positioned to take advantage of a potentially significant market.


Lord Anthony Bamford has been running the company his father Joseph Cyril Bamford founded for over fifty years, and it’s hard to argue against the value of a billionaire’s hand on the tiller when daredevil feats, that might not fly with publicly held companies, are on the menu. A longtime owner of classic Ferraris and Astons, Bamford likes his motorsport and this is one way to compete that his business can pay for, while also serving the purpose of proving that hydrogen can be a useful fuel, especially in the limited settings in which construction vehicles operate. In such applications, the infrastructural issues that haunt the gas in the larger world dissipate quickly, if not as fast as leaking hydrogen, which is absorbed by the atmosphere almost instantly.


JCB


The main problem with top speed runs at Bonneville, to my mind, is that one has a choice of viewing the cars leaving from the starting line then quickly disappearing, or watching them streak by you at V-Max in a millisecond from somewhere up to five miles away from the launch location. Most of us here with JCB choose the former, watching with considerable excitement and anticipation as a white Defender OCTA—with a 4.4-liter turbo V-8, the most powerful Land Rover model ever made—performed its push car duties with a specially designed push plate helping it to quickly shepherd Hydromax to 60 miles per hour, at which point it fell back and the streamliner sped away under its own power. (Gearing is so high in the record chaser that first isn’t much use below that speed.) Within a millisecond it is out of sight, and we await news of its new record along with the crew, all clad in yellow and black, delivered by radio and loudspeaker.


Another problem, aside from Bonneville’s scorching heat, was that the painful effect of pervasive salt dust and suntan lotion that made my eyes burn—not to mention a phone overheating and shutting down several times a day—was the impossibility of actually seeing the pictures I was taking on account of the bright sun. So, you’ll want to excuse the ones I’ve supplied here if they don’t comport with your standards of superior composition or lighting.


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


Home now, none of it mattered. The memory of the Salt Flats and watching the joy when the Hydromax team accomplished its mission will be indelibly burnished in memory. The nervous look on Green’s wife Emma’s face, soon replaced by a great big smile? Priceless.


So, too, all the other incredible people you meet at Bonneville. It’s the ultimate automotive democracy here, with racers, support teams and fans from all backgrounds, political leanings and socio-economic strata, all dedicated to one purpose: driving their cars as fast as possible over 10 miles of packed salt. For every high-ticket team with semi-trucks and air-conditioned RVs there was a backyard mechanic who’d sleep in his truck, his old car’s engine tweaked since last year for a few extra horsepower, its updated aerodynamic aids fashioned out of re-purposed sheet metal. Many come back year after year, meeting up with old friends from seasons past, as well as new friends they’re about to meet.


JCB


I think I’ll remember one old-timer. in particular. Bearded, sun-toasted, and slight of build, he was a friendly fellow who ambled by to watch the Hydromax take off, looking for all the world like Yosemite Sam’s dissolute older brother. He’d had a good day himself and was proud to relate the story of a friend he’d met up with here every year, a 93-year-old car owner who’d turned up for Speed Week his entire adult life until, a couple years back, age left him too unsteady to drive. Still loving the challenge, he’d lent his car out for others to drive, sharing knowledge he’d accumulated over more than half a century attacking the flats. The old man, our new friend explained, had died this year. By way of tribute, his buddies put his ashes in the parachute pack of one of his cars running that day and when it came time to slow down, the chute opened and the dearly departed was scattered across the flats.


If that wasn’t on someone’s bucket list, it should have been.


Jamie Kitman
